title: The Good Shepherd and the Feast of Dedication
summary: Jesus describes himself as the gate for the sheep and the good shepherd who knows his sheep by name and lays down his life for them, unlike thieves and hired hands. Months later, at the Feast of Dedication in winter, the authorities demand that he say plainly whether he is the Christ. He answers that his sheep hear his voice and no one can snatch them from his hand, and that he and the Father are one, and they try to stone him for blasphemy before he withdraws across the Jordan.
story: The chapter follows directly from chapter 9. The Pharisees had thrown a healed man out of the synagogue, and Jesus found him. Now Jesus contrasts the leaders who drive the sheep away with the true shepherd who gathers them. The second half moves ahead to the Feast of Dedication, about two months after Tabernacles, and it brings Jesus' public debates in Jerusalem to their peak. The question “If You are the Christ, tell us plainly” (10:24) is answered with the claim of unity with the Father, and the attempt to stone him shows how near the end has come. Jesus withdraws to where John the Baptist began, and the next chapter will bring him back toward Jerusalem and the cross.
historical:
The Feast of Dedication (10:22), Hanukkah in Hebrew, was not one of the festivals commanded in the law of Moses. It commemorated the rededication of the temple in 164 BC, after the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes had defiled it in 167 BC by setting up pagan worship at the altar. Judas Maccabeus led a Jewish revolt, recaptured Jerusalem, cleansed the sanctuary, and restored the sacrifices; the story is told in 1 Maccabees 4. The feast lasted eight days in the winter month of Kislev (around December) and was also called the Festival of Lights. It celebrated God's deliverance, the purity of the temple, and resistance to rulers who claimed divine honors. In that setting the question of whether Jesus is the Christ, and his claim that the Father consecrated him (10:36), carry special weight.

Solomon's Colonnade (10:23) was a covered walkway along the eastern side of the temple courts, sheltered in winter; the early church later gathered there (Acts 3:11; 5:12). The hostile questioners are again called the Jews, but the chapter itself reports division among them (10:19-21), and many believe (10:42). John's usage points to the leaders pressing Jesus in the temple, not the Jewish people as such, a distinction the church too often forgot.
cultural:
Shepherding was an everyday sight in Judea. Sheep were often kept at night in a walled fold, sometimes shared by several flocks, with a gatekeeper at the entrance. In the morning each shepherd would call out his own sheep, which recognized his voice, and lead them to pasture, walking ahead of them rather than driving them. Travelers' reports from later centuries describe shepherds who slept across the opening of an open fold, becoming the door themselves, a custom that may be much older. A hired hand worked for wages and had no reason to risk his life against wolves or thieves.

In the ancient Near East kings were commonly called shepherds of their people, and Israel's Scriptures use the image for both God and Israel's leaders. Psalm 23 calls the Lord my shepherd. In Ezekiel 34 God condemns Israel's shepherds for feeding themselves and scattering the flock, and promises to shepherd his people himself and to set over them one shepherd, his servant David. Jeremiah 23 makes a similar promise. Jesus' hearers, who had just seen the Pharisees throw out the healed man, would have heard these texts behind his words.
literary: The first part (10:1-21) is what John calls a paroimia, a figure of speech (10:6). It begins with a short parable and then unfolds it through two “I am” sayings: “I am the gate” (10:7, 9) and “I am the good shepherd” (10:11, 14). The images shift freely, as they do in Hebrew prophecy, so Jesus is both the gate and the shepherd. The phrase lay down My life comes five times in 10:11-18, making the shepherd's death the center of the passage. The second part (10:22-42) is a confrontation that echoes the first, with the same themes of sheep, voice, and life, and ends with a return to the place where the Gospel's story began with John the Baptist (1:28), closing Jesus' public ministry of teaching in Jerusalem.

outline.t: I am the gate for the sheep
I am the good shepherd who lays down his life
At the Feast of Dedication: my sheep hear my voice
An attempt to stone him for blasphemy

doctrines.note: “The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep” (10:11). The death of Jesus is for others, and it is voluntary: “No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord” (10:18). He dies willingly and with authority to take his life up again.

“I and the Father are one” (10:30). The Greek word for one is neuter, which suggests one in nature and action rather than one person. The church later drew on this verse against both those who made the Son a lesser being and those who erased the distinction between Father and Son.

Jesus' sheep “will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand” (10:28). Christians in the Reformed tradition read this as teaching that true believers are kept to the end; others stress that it describes those who keep following the shepherd's voice. All agree that the security of the sheep rests on the shepherd, not on themselves.

“I have other sheep that are not of this fold” (10:16). Most read this as the gathering of Gentiles with believing Jews into “one flock and one shepherd.” The church's unity is grounded in one shepherd.

words.note: Poimēn, shepherd. In the Old Testament the image covers God, kings, and leaders. When Jesus says “I am the good shepherd,” he steps into the role God promised to take himself in Ezekiel 34. The word later became a title for church leaders (Ephesians 4:11), whose model is the shepherd who gives his life (compare 1 Peter 5:2-4).

Kalos, good. It can mean morally good, but also noble, beautiful, or excellent. The good shepherd is the model shepherd, the true and worthy one, as opposed to the hired hand. John uses the same word for the good works Jesus showed from the Father (10:32).

Egkainia, dedication or renewal. The word names the feast of the temple's rededication, Hanukkah. Jesus, speaking of himself as the one the Father “sanctified and sent into the world” (10:36), presents himself in the temple at this feast as the one truly set apart for God.

Harpazō, to seize or snatch. The wolf snatches the sheep (10:12), but no one can snatch them from Jesus' hand or from the Father's (10:28-29). The repeated word sets the danger and the protection side by side.

christ: Israel's Scriptures promised a day when God himself would shepherd his scattered people and raise up a shepherd from David's line to care for them (Ezekiel 34:11-24). Jesus claims both roles. He is the good shepherd, and he shares the Father's hand in holding his sheep. Unlike every shepherd before him, he lays down his life for the flock, and he does so in order to take it up again, a clear reference to his death and resurrection. At the feast that celebrated a purified temple and a God-given deliverer, he presents himself as the one consecrated by the Father and sent into the world.

hard.q: When Jesus quotes “I have said you are gods,” is he saying he is divine only in the way all people are?
hard.a:
Jesus answers the charge of blasphemy by quoting Psalm 82:6, where God addresses certain beings as gods. Who those beings are is debated. Many interpreters think the psalm addresses Israel's human judges, who exercised God's authority; some Jewish tradition applied it to Israel at Sinai when they received the law; others think it addresses heavenly beings in God's council. On any of these readings, Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater: if Scripture, which cannot be broken, calls those who received God's word gods, how can it be blasphemy for the one whom the Father sanctified and sent to call himself the Son of God?

Some readers conclude that Jesus is lowering his claim, as if he were only divine in a loose sense. Most interpreters think the opposite, because Jesus immediately says “the Father is in Me, and I am in the Father” (10:38), and the authorities try again to seize him. The argument answers the charge on his opponents' terms while pointing beyond it. The church has confessed from the beginning that Jesus is God in the full sense, and John's Gospel opens and closes with that confession (1:1; 20:28).

questions: Jesus says his sheep know his voice. How have you learned to recognize his voice from other voices?
The hired hand runs because the sheep aren't his. Where might you be caring for others as a hired hand rather than as someone who belongs to them?
What difference does it make to your sense of security that no one can snatch Jesus' sheep out of his hand?
